# 2 Samuel Chapter 24 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 197r–198v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_024_page_001.jpg, 2SA_024_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Once again the LORD's anger blazed against Israel. He stirred up David against them, telling him, "Go and take a census of Israel and Judah."

**2** So the king told Joab, the army commander who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south. Count the people so I can know how many there are."

**3** But Joab replied, "May the LORD your God multiply the people a hundred times over — and may you live to see it, my lord the king! But why on earth does my lord the king want to do this?"

**4** The king's order overruled Joab and the army commanders. So Joab and the commanders left the king's presence to count the people of Israel.

**5** They crossed the Jordan and began at Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the Gad Valley, moving on toward Jazer. **6** They went to Gilead and on to the land of Tahtim-hodshi, then to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon. **7** They reached the fortress of Tyre and all the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites, then headed south through Judah as far as Beersheba.

**8** After nine months and twenty days of traveling through the entire land, they returned to Jerusalem.

**9** Joab reported the census totals to the king: Israel had 800,000 fighting men who could handle a sword, and Judah had 500,000.

**10** But after the census was done, David was stricken with guilt. He said to the LORD, "I have committed a terrible sin by doing this. Please, LORD, forgive your servant's guilt — I have been an utter fool."

**11** The next morning, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, David's personal seer: **12** "Go and tell David, 'This is what the LORD says: I am giving you three choices. Pick one, and I will carry it out.'"

**13** Gad went to David and laid out the options: "Do you want seven years of famine across your land? Or three months on the run from your enemies, with them in hot pursuit? Or three days of plague sweeping through the country? Think it over and tell me what answer to bring back to the one who sent me."

**14** David answered Gad, "This is agonizing. But let us fall into the LORD's hands — his mercy is great. Do not let me fall into human hands."

**15** So the LORD sent a plague on Israel. It began that morning and continued until the appointed time, and seventy thousand people died across the land, from Dan to Beersheba.

**16** But when the angel reached out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD was grieved by the devastation and said to the angel who was killing the people, "Enough! Pull back your hand." The angel of the LORD was standing right there at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

**17** When David saw the angel striking down the people, he cried out to the LORD: "I am the one who sinned! I am the one who did wrong! But these people — they are just sheep! What did they do? Turn your hand against me and my family instead."

**18** That same day Gad came to David and said, "Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."

**19** So David went up, following Gad's instructions, just as the LORD had commanded.

**20** When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his officials approaching, he came out and bowed facedown before the king.

**21** "Why has my lord the king come to visit his servant?" Araunah asked. David said, "To buy your threshing floor, so I can build an altar to the LORD and stop this plague."

**22** Araunah said to David, "Take it, my lord the king! Offer whatever you think best. Here — take the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and ox yokes for firewood."

**23** Araunah offered it all to the king. "May the LORD your God be pleased with you," he said.

**24** But the king replied, "No — I insist on paying you a fair price. I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

**25** David built an altar to the LORD there and sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings. The LORD answered the prayers for the land, and the plague was lifted from Israel.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — Who incited David?** This is one of the Bible's great theological puzzles. The Hebrew says the LORD's anger burned and *he* incited David. But the Chronicler, telling the same story centuries later, says *Satan* incited David (1 Chr 21:1). The same event, two different agents. This is not a contradiction to be explained away — it is a window into Israel's evolving theology. The earlier text attributes everything to God, even destructive impulses. The later text introduces an intermediary figure. Both are canonical. Both are true in their own way.

**Verse 10 — "David's heart struck him":** The Hebrew is astonishing in its physicality — David's own heart *hits* him. Conscience is not gentle here. It is a fist to the chest. David does not gradually realize he was wrong; he is slammed by the knowledge.

**Verse 14 — "his mercy is great":** David's reasoning is extraordinary. Given a choice between famine (which depends on weather and economics — partly in human hands), military defeat (entirely in human hands), or plague (entirely in God's hands), David chooses the one option where only God controls the outcome. His logic: God can be merciful. Humans cannot be trusted with that kind of power. This is the theology of a man who has been both the recipient and the perpetrator of human cruelty.

**Verse 16 — "the LORD was grieved":** The Hebrew *vayyinnachem* is often translated "relented," but the root means something closer to "felt grief" or "was moved to compassion." God stops the plague not because he runs out of anger but because he is overwhelmed by pity. The destroying angel's hand is stayed by divine heartbreak.

**Verse 17 — "they are just sheep":** David's plea is raw: punish me, not them. He calls his own people "sheep" — not as an insult but as a claim of responsibility. A shepherd does not blame the flock. Whatever David's sin in taking the census, the people did not choose it.

**Verse 24 — "that cost me nothing":** This single sentence has shaped how Jews and Christians think about worship, giving, and sacrifice for three thousand years. Real worship costs something. If it doesn't hurt, if it doesn't require something of you, it isn't an offering — it's a gesture. David gets this. He insists on paying.

**Verse 25 — the ending:** The book of 2 Samuel ends not with triumph or death but with a sacrifice on a threshing floor. This threshing floor will become the Temple Mount. The place where God's judgment stopped becomes the place where God's presence dwells. Destruction becomes worship. The plague ground becomes holy ground.

*— PNEUMA*
